title: How Write-Ahead Logs Guarantee Your Bank Balance Never Vanishes During a Blackout — Engineering Cheat Sheet
subtitle: Ensuring transactional durability through sequential append-only persistence.
summary: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) ensures ACID compliance by recording transactions to non-volatile storage before modifying the primary data files. This mechanism guarantees durability, allowing systems to reconstruct state after a crash by replaying committed logs.

key_concepts.name: Write-Ahead Protocol
key_concepts.detail: Data modifications must be flushed to the persistent WAL file on disk before the corresponding page in the data file is updated, guaranteeing crash recovery atomicity.

key_concepts.name: Sequential I/O vs Random I/O
key_concepts.detail: WAL leverages sequential disk writes, which are significantly faster than random access writes required to update fragmented database data files, optimizing throughput under heavy write loads.

key_concepts.name: Checkpointing
key_concepts.detail: The process of flushing dirty pages from memory to disk and truncating the log. It minimizes recovery time (RTO) by limiting the amount of log to replay.

code_cheatsheet.explanation: Essential syscall to force the OS kernel to flush file buffers to physical storage, ensuring the log entry is actually durable.

code_cheatsheet.code: with open('wal.log', 'ab') as f: f.write(txn_data + b'\n'); f.flush(); os.fsync(f.fileno())
code_cheatsheet.explanation: Demonstrates the mandatory sequence: append transaction to log, flush buffers, then perform the heavy `fsync` to guarantee durability before updating application state.

best_practices: Always use 'fsync' or synchronous write flags to bypass OS/disk controller caches for true durability.
Place WAL files on dedicated physical storage (e.g., NVMe) to prevent I/O contention with data files.
Monitor 'checkpoint' latency and frequency; frequent checkpoints increase disk wear, while infrequent ones spike recovery time.
Implement log rotation or archiving (e.g., Postgres WAL archiving) to prevent disk space exhaustion.

interview_qa.question: If a transaction is committed, but the power cuts before the data file is updated, how does the system recover?
interview_qa.answer: Upon restart, the database engine scans the WAL from the last checkpoint. It re-applies all committed but unpersisted transactions to the data files, effectively 'replaying' the history to bring the system back to the precise state of the last committed transaction.
